title: Biochemistry for medicine: enzymes, energy and pH
note: Enzymes are protein catalysts that lower activation energy without being used up. Cells extract energy from fuel in stages (glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, the electron transport chain) and store it as ATP. Blood pH is held near 7.4 by buffers, the lungs (minutes) and the kidneys (hours to days).

read.title: Why breathing changes blood pH
text: Cells constantly make carbon dioxide as they burn fuel. In red blood cells, the enzyme carbonic anhydrase quickly joins CO2 with water to form carbonic acid, which splits into a hydrogen ion and bicarbonate. Because the reaction runs both ways, the blood's acidity depends on how much CO2 is present and how much bicarbonate is available to soak up hydrogen ions.

When blood pH is normal, about 7.35 to 7.45, bicarbonate outnumbers carbonic acid roughly 20 to 1. Chemical buffers respond within seconds, but they only absorb a disturbance; they do not remove it. The lungs act next. Breathing faster blows off CO2 and pulls the reaction away from acid, raising pH within minutes. Breathing slower retains CO2 and lowers pH.

The kidneys are the slow but powerful partner. Over hours to days they secrete hydrogen ions into urine and reclaim or make bicarbonate. This is why a problem that starts in the lungs is compensated by the kidneys, and a metabolic problem is compensated first by a change in breathing.
